analysis.one_liner: Bans advertising targeted to individuals using their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill got no committee action and died in the Senate with a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit advertisers and the platforms and brokers that deliver their ads from targeting ads to individuals based on personal information — browsing history, contact details, or any data linked to a person or their devices. Ads based on the content a person is currently viewing or searching, or on broad location like a state or city, would still be allowed. It gives the Federal Trade Commission power to enforce the ban, lets state attorneys general sue, and creates a private right to sue for $100 to $5,000 per violation, with pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, whose browsing, location, and personal details could no longer be packaged and sold to aim ads at them individually.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits advertisers and advertising facilitators from targeting ads based on personal information linked to an individual or their devices, and bars sharing the lists, contact information, and identifiers used to do it.

Allows only contextual ads (based on what a person is currently viewing or searching) and targeting by broad recognized place such as a state or congressional district, and bars reuse of contextual-ad data for further targeting.

Enforces the ban through the FTC — including over common carriers and nonprofits — through state attorneys general, and through a private right of action with $100–$5,000 per-violation damages and attorney's fees, and makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims.

analysis.who_pays: Digital advertising companies and large platforms whose core business is collecting personal data to sell targeted ad placement, plus advertisers that lose a precise marketing tool.

drawbacks.text: Many small businesses and nonprofits use cheap, precisely targeted online ads to reach customers; a ban on individual targeting would make reaching niche audiences more expensive for them even as it protects privacy.
The private right of action with per-violation damages and a ban on arbitration and class-action waivers [S2] could generate substantial litigation against companies for technical violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gain for hundreds of millions of users is large and the ban is carefully drawn — contextual and location-level advertising remain legal — but the costs are real for small advertisers who relied on precise targeting to compete with big brands, and a per-violation damages regime invites some abusive litigation. On balance the consumer benefit outweighs the cost, though the litigation provisions would likely need tuning.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Banning Surveillance Advertising Act of 2023 on September 18, 2023, for himself and Sen. Cory Booker.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

One senator — Sen. Booker, listed as the bill's single cosponsor — joined it; the committee took no further action on the bill, and the 118th Congress ended without a markup, floor vote, or House companion action recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Digital ad platforms, data brokers, and advertisers that profit from targeted advertising; internet users gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Digital ad industry and big platforms

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only additional Senate supporter.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Digital advertising industry (major platforms and ad-tech firms)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against individual-targeting bans and similar privacy legislation in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Senate Democrats (1 of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsored beyond the sponsor); no Republican or other member signed on, and the Democratic-run committee declined to move it either.

industries.industry: Digital advertising and ad-tech (Google, Meta, ad exchanges, data brokers)
industries.note: Their core revenue depends on collecting personal information to aim ads at individuals; the bill makes that business model illegal. Ending it means users stop paying for 'free' services with perpetual behavioral surveillance.

industries.industry: Large consumer platforms and common carriers
industries.note: They would lose targeted-ad income but could still sell contextual and location-level ads; the bill also expressly extends FTC enforcement to common carriers and nonprofits, closing a long-standing jurisdictional gap.
The bill outlaws precisely targeted ads, which many small advertisers use as a cheap way to reach niche customers; they would shift to costlier contextual placement.
